title: Compositions and methods for use in three dimensional model printing

report.headline: Dead patent with a future: Stratasys's expired multi-material inkjet 3D printing method scores 91/100 because the field is busy and still citing it, but a dense thicket of newer patents means it is a starting point for research, not an open road.
report.what_it_is: This patent covers printing an object with two or more different liquid materials, each sprayed from its own inkjet head, and mixing them in controlled amounts so different parts of the object end up harder, softer or chemically different. The materials are then cured, giving one printed part whose properties change from one side to the other, like a built-in composite.

why_it_died.text: It did not die early or for lack of interest. It ran its full term and ended on 2021-03-12. The owner, a large company, kept paying every maintenance fee until the end, which suggests they valued it. That is why the 'died for money, not merit' part of the score is only half marks: it simply aged out.

case_for.point: The field appears very alive. The patent has been cited by 404 later filings, and 60 of those have priority dates from 2019 on. That earned full marks for 'field still alive' and 'recent momentum'.

Serious companies are still building on this idea, including General Electric (13 filings since 2019), Inkbit, Applied Materials and Xerox. That signals real industrial interest in multi-material inkjet parts.
Others keep filing on it even after it expired. 15 unrelated filings with priority dates after 2021-03-12 cite it, so people see it as foundational prior work.
It was broad and important when granted. Examiners cited it against 111 later applications, and it was filed in 5 jurisdictions, which earned strong breadth and examiner-relevance scores.

case_against.point: Stratasys did not walk away. It filed 90 later patents citing this one that may still be in force, so the newer improvements a product would need may still be owned by the original company.
Heavy competition from well-funded players. GE, Applied Materials and others are active here, so a startup may face both patent and market pressure from much larger companies.
Citations show interest, not proven demand. High citation counts do not tell you who would pay for multi-material printed parts or how much.
The patent shows the idea, not the recipe. Ink chemistry, curing settings and nozzle control details likely have to be rebuilt from scratch.

blockers.point: Possible later patents from the original owner: 90 Stratasys filings citing this one may still be in force and may cover modern versions of the method.
Possible later patents from other owners: 106 patents by others were cited against this one and may still be in force.
Materials may stay locked up even if the method is open. Specific resins, inks or process parameters may still be patented separately.
Missing know-how. Expect real R&D time and cost to get reliable multi-material prints, since the patent does not include manufacturing details.

assumption_to_test.assumption: There is a specific customer group (for example, medical device, footwear or prototyping teams) that needs parts with properties that vary across the part, and that is willing to pay a startup rather than buy from Stratasys or similar large vendors.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The technical interest is clearly proven by citations and big-company filings, but none of the evidence shows who pays or why they would pick a newcomer over well-funded incumbents. If no buyer exists that incumbents underserve, the patent landscape question does not matter.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, run 15 short interviews with engineers in 2-3 target industries using LinkedIn outreach (cost near $0). Ask what multi-material parts they make today, what they pay, and what is broken. In parallel, put up a $100-$300 landing page offering graded-property prototype parts with a 'request a quote' form and drive targeted ads to it. Success looks like at least 5 interviewees describing a painful, paid problem and at least a few real quote requests.

attorney_questions: Which of the 90 later Stratasys filings citing US7300619B2 appear to still be in force, and do any of them appear to cover the multi-material inkjet method we plan to use?
Among the 106 patents by other owners cited against this one, and the recent filings by GE, Inkbit and Applied Materials, which are worth a closer look for our specific product and materials?
If we use commercially available resins or develop our own, what separate material or process-parameter patents should we check before choosing an ink chemistry?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: The underlying field, multi-material inkjet-deposited 3D printing, still draws sustained technical attention well after this patent's term ended.
Large industrial players are actively filing in adjacent areas. General Electric leads recent citing filings, and Inkbit is a notable specialist in multi-material inkjet.

The original owner valued the patent through its full term and protected it internationally, which suggests it was commercially important to them. This does not prove the technology generates revenue today.
Examiners frequently cited it as prior art, which marks it as a foundational reference that later applicants must design around or build upon.

read.who_is_active: Recent citing filers include General Electric (13), Inkbit (6), Applied Materials (3), Xerox (2), Raytheon (1) and Ossur (1), spanning industrial, semiconductor-equipment, defense and medical-device players.
read.market_read: Citation momentum since 2019 and a revival score of 91/100 indicate that multi-phase inkjet 3D printing remains an active, contested technical area with well-resourced participants. A founder should treat this as evidence of live interest and competition rather than proven market size, and should get legal review of the current patent landscape before acting.
